attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his Substack post, summarising his view of the commentary.

semantics.note: Keeps 'most' and 'one or both', and states the two ideas as he gave them. It is a firm claim about the commentary at that time.

contract.note: Plain reading: more than half of distinct items over Dec 20–21, with 'ignored' meaning omitted. That reading is ordinary and fair. The result depends on a sampling frame he never named.

evidence.note: Chollet's Dec 20 post on ARC Prize does address benchmark insufficiency. It is one counterexample. It cannot show whether most commentary covered the ideas.
A Dec 20 Ars Technica report focused on benchmark scores and did not develop either idea. It fits his observation but is a single hand-picked item, not a measure of the majority.

reviews.rationale: The claim is about the share of all commentary. The packet has two hand-picked items pointing in opposite directions, with no sampling frame and no content analysis. Selected examples cannot set a population proportion, so the evidence neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own forecast in his post. Nothing is quoted from anyone else.

semantics.note: 'Almost nobody will give' is an unhedged forecast. Its scope is the 2025 AGI claimants named in the previous sentence. The separate claim that 'a lot' of people would declare AGI is rightly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'almost nobody' as 'only exceptional cases' is ordinary and fair. Counting definitions given later in 2025 is a reasonable scope choice. The result depends on a claimant denominator he did not define.

evidence.note: Cowen's April 2025 AGI declaration shows qualifying claimants existed. The post itself avoids a definition ('know it when I see it'), but one case does not set a share.
Cowen gave a threshold in July 2025 (beats experts on 90% of tasks). That is one counterexample within 2025. One exception cannot refute 'almost nobody'.

An archive dated before the cutoff records a June 2025 claimant who used a Turing-test criterion. The original post could not be retrieved and the account's influencer status is unverified. It is another isolated example.

reviews.rationale: The horizon (end of 2025) has passed. The packet shows that claimants existed and that a couple of them gave criteria, but it has no list of claimants and no systematic coding of who gave definitions. The evidence cannot show whether definitions were exceptional or common, so the forecast is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence describing his reaction to the o3 presentation.

semantics.note: Keeps 'suggested to me', so the claim reports his own impression. It is not an objective claim about technical progress.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to make his personal impression an objective claim, and sets no scoring criterion. Scoring on technical progress would overstate his commitment.

reviews.rationale: The statement reports what the presentation suggested to him personally. No outside evidence can confirm or refute that impression, and 'remotely solved' has no threshold. The packet rightly offers no outcome evidence.
